label: header

label: text
text: The "New York Times" expresses the opinion that the war debt settlements cannot endure. It adds:—

label: text
text: "Nothing can be more certain than that two generations of Europe will not, without protest, continue paying vast sums to the United States. It is equally certain that it would be good Business for us to accept virtually for cash in hand the present value of the debts as soon as any sound and skillful plan for funding them can be elaborated and agreed to"

label: paragraph_title
text: French Debt.

label: text
text: The settlement is on a basis of 62 years, with the payment of $30,000,000 annually for the first two years, $82,500,000 annually for the next two years, and graduating thereafter to a maximum of $125,000,000 annually.

label: text
text: Washington, April 29: A settlement has been reached for the funding of the French debt. Terms. Detailed.

label: text
text: It is calculated that the payments will aggregate $6,847,000,000. No interest will charged for the first five years, but thereafter the rate of interest will gradually increase from one per cent. in the first 10 years to 3½ per cent. in the last 22 years.

label: text
text: There is said to be no safety clause.

label: paragraph_title
text: KOREA EXCITED.

label: paragraph_title
text: WEEPING FOR THE LATE EMPEROR

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: This morning "High" publishes reports from Seoul, according to which the ex-Emperor's death resulted in abnormal excitement in the Korean capital. The Police are most active in controlling the tremendous crowds which are collecting daily in the front of the palace for the purpose of expressing condolence by weeping in accordance with Korean custom.

label: text
text: It is reported that the Korean police are becoming most excited and killed one Japanese and seriously injured another with their sabres yesterday whilst attempting to regulate the crowds.

label: paragraph_title
text: POLAR RACE.

label: text
text: BYRD EXPEDITION AT KING'S

label: text
text: TWO AEROPLANES TO BE USED.

label: text
text: (Reuter's Service.)

label: text
text: The Byrd Polar Expedition has arrived at King's Bay, Spitzbergen.

label: text
text: The ship Chantier carries two aeroplanes, with which it is intended to fly to the Pole from a base 400 miles away.

label: paragraph_title
text: Byrd's Expectations.

label: text
text: The Chantier, which has a speed of nearly ten knots, besides carrying the two planes, has all the other equipment required for the Polaris expedition. Her hold is filled with coal, and a cargo of 4,500 gallons of airplane fuel will be taken along. Food supplies for six months will be carried. The fuel supply is expected to permit approximately 10,000 miles of flying. The most modern navigational equipment will be installed in the two planes Byrd will use. The sun compass, which was used by Byrd and MacMillan with success on the expedition last year, has been improved during the winter, and an earth induction compass, a highly sensitive instrument, will be carried in the planes.

label: paragraph_title
text: The Base.

label: text
text: Commander Byrd is confident that a landing can be made at Cape Morris. Jesup during May. During this period everything is covered with snow, which he regards as safer than ice formations. Though the cold is more intense during May, the better wind and fog conditions will compensate for this drawback. All flights from the base at Cape Morris Jesup will carry the explorers over territory which is unexplored and if conditions are not such as will permit flights to the Pole, explorations can be made in this region, which has never been seen by man.

label: paragraph_title
text: Radio Experts:

label: text
text: Commander Byrd expects to keep in constant radio communication with his base ship at King's Bay. Two experts on short wave length equipment will be in the party. No attempts will be made to broadcast over great distances. Communication with the world will be through relayed messages from the base ship to Green Harbour.

label: text
text: "Our expedition," Byrd said, "has been conservatively planned. We are not going to make any wild dishes to the Pole, but we hope to reach that objective if possible to do so. Our hope is to show that serial navigation of the Polar region is possible. With this accomplished, we will have made a great advance in the development of commercial aviation."

label: text
text: A wireless message from Point Barrow announces the safe arrival of Nielsen, the pilot of the Wilkins North Polar Expendition.

A score of persons have been drowned through the collapse of a temporary bridge over the River Okhta ten miles from Leningrad.
(Heuter's Service.)

label: text
text:
The coal outlook is admittedly dark, but there is some hope in this darkest hour before the dawn. The miners' leaders were early this morning discussing the policy with the General Council of the Trade Union Congress, and it is learned that the whole Trade Union movement will solidly support the miners' demands.
Simultaneously, the owners conferred separately, and their Committee later saw Mr. Baldwin. All negotiations are most secret, but much depends on the latest attitude of the owners.

label: text
text: The Trade Union Conference has adopted a resolution in favour of general support of the miners. No decision regarding a gen.

label: text
text: Though the coal negotiations are still continuing, late in the evening the gravity situation was indicated by Mr. J. H. Thomas (Labourite, Derby), expressing the opinion that it was 1,000 to one on a stoppage, adding that if they were inch apart last night they were separated by an arm's length to night.

label: text
text: The coal discussions continued till after midnight when the Prime Minister, after a discussion, lasting 2½ hours, with the owners' representatives, met the Committees of the miners and the Trade Union Congress, and after a brief sitting the latter conference was adjourned till later in the morning.

label: text
text: It is stated that the owners will submit specific proposals to the Prime Minister after which he will again confer with the joint Committee of the Trade Union Congress and the Miners' Executive.

label: text
text:
It is understood that the Miners' Executive have definitely rejected the eight-hour day proposal and that the question which the Prime Minister discussed with the owners as the immediate issue was the suspension of the employers' notices.
It is reported that the Prime Minister indicated that he is prepared to consider an extension of State financial assistance for a few days in order to give further time for negotiation, provided that the owners suspended their notices.

label: text
text: It is understood that Mr. Baldwin is convinced that there will not be a con&stoppage.

label: text

label: text
text: HEAVY PENALTIES:

label: text
text: (Reuter's American Service.)

label: text
text: Both Houses of Congress have approved of the Bill for the restriction of the sugar crop and the establishment of a sugar intelligence Committee.

label: text
text: The Bill provides a fine for every bag of sugar milled over each planter's quota and a fine of £2,000 a day on mills violating the decree fixing the date for the commencement of the sugar harvest.

label: paragraph_title
text: PEKING COMMUNISTS

label: text
text:
Peking, April 21.
The activities of Communists in Peking have been restricted to some extent. It is learned that they have decided to keep a few moderate members in Peking exclusively to enlist and train new members, and to send skillful workers to conduct propaganda among the employees of the Government railways. The majority of Communists leaving Peking will proceed to Chengchow, Kaifong, and Talyuanfu, the rest will travel along the Peking-Mukden and Tiantsin-Pukow lines with the exception of a few who will start work on the Peking-Sulyuan line. Most of the comrades now remaining in Peking have removed their residences in order to escape the attention of the police.—"Kuo Wen New Agency."
